title: Protection and security
relevance: Interviewers use protection vs security, least privilege, access matrices, malware distinctions, and defense-in-depth to test whether candidates understand how systems limit access and resist threats.

phases.goal: Establish what protection and security are, their goals, and the principle of least privilege.

must_hit.point: Protection is an internal mechanism controlling how processes and users access system resources; security defends against external and internal threats and sets policy at the boundary.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate separates protection (access control mechanisms) from security (threat defense and policy).

must_hit.point: The goal of protection is that each object is accessed correctly and only by processes that are allowed, enforcing a well-defined set of operations per object.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions correct, authorized access and allowed operations on objects like memory, files, devices, CPU.

must_hit.point: Principle of least privilege: every program and user gets just the privileges needed to do its job, and no more, limiting damage from bugs or compromise.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States least privilege and that excess rights increase blast radius when something fails.

probes: What is the difference between protection and security in an OS?
What is the principle of least privilege, and why does it matter?

hints.1: Think internal access control versus defending against attackers and misuse.
hints.2: Protection provides mechanisms; security sets policy and guards the boundary.
hints.3: Least privilege means only the rights needed for the job—no more—so a buggy or compromised component does less damage.

phases.goal: Explain protection domains, the access matrix and its implementations, violation categories, attacks, and malware types.

must_hit.point: A protection domain is a set of access rights, each an <object, {allowed operations}> pair; a process runs in a domain and may only perform operations that domain grants.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines domain as a set of object–operation rights that bound what a process can do.

must_hit.point: The access matrix has rows as domains, columns as objects; entry (i, j) is the operations domain i may invoke on object j; systems implement it as ACLs (by column) or capabilities (by row).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes matrix shape and ACL-per-object versus capability-per-domain compact forms.

must_hit.point: Security violations include breaches of confidentiality, integrity, and availability, plus theft of service and denial of service.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists CIA triad plus unauthorized use of resources and preventing legitimate use.

must_hit.point: Common attack methods include masquerading, replay, man-in-the-middle, and session hijacking.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names spoofing identity, resending messages, sitting in the data path, and stealing an authenticated session.

must_hit.point: Program threats: trojan looks legitimate but hides a payload and does not self-replicate; virus is self-replicating code in a host program; worm self-replicates across systems on its own; spyware collects info; trap door/backdoor bypasses authentication.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts trojan vs virus vs worm on host and self-replication, and mentions spyware and backdoors.

probes: How does the access matrix model protection, and how do ACLs and capabilities relate to it?
Walk through the CIA triad and the other classic violation types.
How do a virus, a worm, and a trojan horse differ?

hints.1: Start from who can do what to which object, then how that table is stored.
hints.2: Rows are domains, columns are objects; ACLs group by object, capabilities by domain.
hints.3: Virus needs a host and execution to spread; worm spreads alone; trojan neither self-replicates nor needs a host—it relies on the user running it.

phases.goal: Contrast compact realizations of the access matrix and how defenses address different threat layers.

must_hit.point: Access-control lists implement the matrix by column (per object: who may access it); capabilities implement it by row (per domain: what it may touch).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Clearly maps ACL to object-centric and capability to domain-centric views of the same matrix.

must_hit.point: Cryptography protects confidentiality and authenticity with keys; firewalls barrier trusted and untrusted networks and inspect traffic (packet-filter, application-proxy, system-call).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates crypto (message secrecy/authenticity) from firewalls (boundary traffic control and types).

probes: When would you think in terms of ACLs versus capabilities?
What roles do cryptography and firewalls play in defense?

hints.1: Both encode the same who-can-do-what model, stored differently.
hints.2: Ask whether you index by object (who may touch it) or by domain (what may it touch).
hints.3: ACL = column/per-object list; capability = row/per-domain list of rights.

phases.goal: Apply threat models and layered defenses, including defense in depth.

must_hit.point: System and network threats include port scanning, DoS/DDoS, and SYN attacks against the TCP handshake.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names probing open services, flooding (including distributed), and SYN connection-flood tricks.

must_hit.point: Defense in depth must be enforced at four levels—physical, human, operating system, and network—because security is only as strong as the weakest link.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists physical, human, OS, and network layers and the weakest-link idea.

probes: What system and network threats would you watch for beyond malware?
What does defense in depth mean, and at what levels must it be applied?

hints.1: Think probing services and flooding resources, not only malicious programs.
hints.2: Defense must hold at physical sites, people, the OS, and the network.
hints.3: Four levels: physical, human, operating system, network—weakest link limits the whole.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Both implement the access matrix compactly: ACLs by column (per object, who may access it) and capabilities by row (per domain, what it may touch).

Cryptography protects confidentiality and authenticity of messages with keys so only intended parties can read and verify senders; firewalls place a barrier between trusted and untrusted networks, limiting and inspecting traffic (packet-filter, application-proxy, system-call).

gotchas.trap: Treating protection and security as the same thing.
gotchas.correction: Protection is the internal access-control mechanism; security defends against threats and sets policy at the boundary—protection provides mechanisms, security the policy.

gotchas.trap: Confusing trojan, virus, and worm under the malware umbrella.
gotchas.correction: A virus needs a host and an execution to spread; a worm needs neither and spreads on its own; a trojan neither self-replicates nor needs a host—it relies on the user running it willingly.

gotchas.trap: Thinking confidentiality, integrity, and availability cover all classic violation categories.
gotchas.correction: Beyond the CIA triad, attacks also include theft of service (unauthorized use of resources) and denial of service (preventing legitimate use).
